## What Is an Employer of Record in Ivory Coast


If you’re planning to hire in Ivory Coast without a local entity on the ground, you need to know who actually carries the legal and compliance weight of that employment relationship. That’s the role an employer of record plays, and it’s worth understanding exactly what it covers before you commit to a hire.


An employer of record (EOR) is a third-party organization that becomes the legal employer for your workers in Ivory Coast, while you keep full control over their day-to-day work. Instead of registering your own entity with Ivory Coast’s authorities, the EOR holds that legal relationship: it signs the local employment contract, runs payroll, and manages CNPS registration and contributions on your behalf. That distinction matters in Ivory Coast, since the Labour Code generally expects formal written contracts and social security enrollment regardless of how informal hiring norms can look in practice, and missing those steps is what exposes foreign employers to misclassification penalties or a CNPS audit. For a company with no legal presence in the country, an EOR is generally the faster path to a compliant hire, often in days instead of the weeks or months a local entity setup requires. You remain the day-to-day employer, directing the work itself, while the EOR absorbs the contracts, payroll, and compliance burden that would otherwise sit entirely on you.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Ivory Coast


Hiring directly in Ivory Coast means taking on the full weight of the Labour Code yourself, in a market where informal employment is common but the law still expects written, formal compliance. For a foreign employer unfamiliar with local enforcement norms, that gap between custom and law is where risk lives.


Under Ivory Coast’s Labour Code, contracts are generally expected to be formalized in writing and specify whether the role is indefinite-term or fixed-term. Employers typically register workers with the Caisse Nationale de Prevoyance Sociale (CNPS), Ivory Coast’s social security body, and remit[CNPS contribution rates](https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/ivory-coast/individual/other-taxes) covering pensions, family benefits, and workplace injury coverage, on top of probation, notice, wage, leave, and severance obligations.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Ivory Coast: Which Is Right for You


You now know what Ivory Coast’s compliance rules demand and what each path costs. The question left is which one fits your company today, and that comes down to three factors: how fast you need to be compliant, how many people you’re hiring, and how much ongoing legal and administrative work you want to own.


The right choice generally comes down to timeline, headcount, and how much legal and administrative overhead you want to own. An employer of record (EOR) helps you get compliant in Ivory Coast fast, with Bolto onboarding new hires in as little as 48 hours and no need to register your own entity, which makes it the practical choice for a first hire, a small pilot team, or any plan still being tested. A local entity makes more sense once your headcount is large enough to absorb the fixed costs of incorporation, local legal counsel, and accounting infrastructure, and you want full control over benefits design and long-term HR policy. The tradeoff runs in both directions: an EOR carries some vendor dependency and less flexibility on customized equity or benefits structures, while a local entity means you alone are responsible for CNPS registration, contract compliance, and every filing deadline going forward. For most foreign employers hiring one to a handful of people in Ivory Coast, that balance tips toward an EOR, with a local entity becoming worth the investment only once scale warrants the fixed overhead.
